reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: Formerly termed idiopathic bronchiolitis obliterans organising pneumonia (BOOP).
Presents subacutely over weeks with dry cough, breathlessness, low-grade fever, malaise and weight loss, frequently mistaken for a community-acquired pneumonia that fails to resolve on antibiotics.
HRCT shows patchy, often peripheral or peribronchial consolidation that may be migratory; the reversed halo (atoll) sign is suggestive but not specific.
Histology reveals intraluminal plugs of granulation tissue (Masson bodies) filling distal airspaces and alveolar ducts with preserved lung architecture.
Diagnosis of cryptogenic disease requires exclusion of secondary organising pneumonia due to infection, drugs, radiation, connective tissue disease, aspiration or malignancy.
Bronchoalveolar lavage typically shows a mixed cellularity with lymphocytosis and often foamy macrophages.
There is an excellent response to corticosteroids, but relapse during dose reduction is common and usually responds to re-treatment.
Pulmonary function is normal or shows a restrictive defect, and transfer factor is commonly reduced.
reference.pathophysiology: Alveolar epithelial injury triggers an exuberant organising repair response in which fibroblasts and myofibroblasts migrate into alveolar spaces, ducts and terminal bronchioles to form plugs of loose connective tissue. Because the underlying lung architecture is preserved, the process is typically reversible, distinguishing it from the fibrosing interstitial pneumonias. When no precipitating cause is identified the disorder is termed cryptogenic.
additionalDifferentials: Pulmonary vasculitis or diffuse alveolar haemorrhage
additionalInvestigations: HRCT thorax to characterise distribution and migratory nature of consolidation
Bronchoalveolar lavage to exclude infection and characterise cellularity
Transbronchial or surgical lung biopsy for histological confirmation
Autoimmune serology to exclude connective tissue disease
Review of drug and radiation exposure
Pulmonary function tests with transfer factor
Inflammatory markers and cultures to exclude active infection
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or fulminant organising pneumonia with respiratory failure
Haemoptysis suggesting an alternative diagnosis such as vasculitis
Failure to respond to corticosteroids, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Features suggesting underlying malignancy or systemic vasculitis
reference.prognosis: Most patients recover fully with corticosteroid therapy; relapses during dose reduction are frequent but usually respond to re-treatment, and only a minority follow a rapidly progressive fibrosing course.
pitfalls: Repeated courses of antibiotics for 'non-resolving pneumonia' that delay the diagnosis
Failing to search for a secondary cause before labelling the disease cryptogenic
Withdrawing corticosteroids too rapidly and precipitating relapse
Overlooking a rapidly progressive fibrotic variant that requires escalated treatment
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
ATS/ERS international multidisciplinary classification of the idiopathic interstitial pneumonias
management: Treat with oral corticosteroids as the mainstay, typically producing rapid clinical and radiological improvement, followed by a gradual taper

Manage the frequent relapses on dose reduction by re-escalating corticosteroids, adding steroid-sparing immunosuppressants such as azathioprine or ciclosporin, or a macrolide for relapsing or refractory disease
Before labelling disease cryptogenic, exclude secondary organising pneumonia due to infection, drugs, radiation, connective tissue disease, aspiration or malignancy
Provide supportive care including supplemental oxygen and pulmonary rehabilitation where breathlessness limits function
Monitor response and relapse with serial HRCT and pulmonary function tests including transfer factor, while watching for corticosteroid adverse effects
Manage through a respiratory or interstitial lung disease multidisciplinary team
